A good deal of work was also done to improve the roads leading from the village to the wharf. A large quantity of rock was blasted, and the roadway was finished by the addition of a layer of sand six inches thick. Ditches and culverts were built where found desirable.
I would point out that the government wharf at Chiliwack is what might be termed a moveable feast. Owing to the lack of dredging there, we often have to move the spot of gravel which is called a wharf a Mr. IPUGSLEY.
House in committee on Bill (No. Ill) respecting the Dominion Millers' Association -Mr. Harris.
On section 2 as amended-powers to hold real estate.

This is the matter to which I called attention the other night. I do not know who takes charge of this Bill on behalf of the government, but I urge again the point I mentioned. Instead of 'for the purposes of their business,' it

should read, 'for the purpose of their undertaking.'

I think 'business' is rather more applicable to a company of this character than 'undertaking,' particularly as, in other sections of the Bill, 'business' is the word used. For instance, section 3, subsection (a) authorizes the association to carry on the 'business of purchasing, selling,' and so on.

I cannot see it in that way. What I called attention to the other night is that in the case of railway Bills, the object is to confine them to the business they undertake, and in these Bills we say 'for the purposes of their undertaking.' This form of words has acquired a definite signification in connection with railway charters, and it seems to me very much better to adopt the same form of language in connection with a Bill of this kind. Of course, if the government think otherwise, I have nothing more to say.
It is like chips in porridge.
Well, chips in porridge are uncomfortable.
But they do not change the taste.

Very true, but they are very inconvenient. For my part, if it is legislative porridge, I would rather have the chips out. And, if I may express an opinion on the subject, I think we are not quite as particular as we ought to be in reference to legislation that we pass. The observations I offer from time to time-they are very infrequent as it happens-are with the object of making legislation better where possible. However, I recognize the	fact that the government
.take the responsibility. Still, I do not regard this as a 'chip in porridge,' but as a matter of substantial importance. We should bear in mind that our legislation gets into the courts from time to time, and, if we have one phraseology in one statute and another in another statute, in cases in which the meaning is substantially the same, we inevitably lead to litigation and to confusion. And that, as I say, is not a matter of 'chips in porridge,' but a matter of substantial importance.

I agree with the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley). The hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox), of course, is quite right when he says that we use the word 'undertaking' in relation to railway matters. But this is a different thing, and I think what we wish to say is better covered by the word 'business.' It is a technical point, and really it would be hard to tell the difference, but
there is a difference. The railway is an undertaking; this says: 'Business or businesses.' I think the words-: 'For the purpose of its business,' covers the object better than the words: 'For the purpose of its undertaking.'
If that be the case, why do they put the same words in a power company? Because we passed one or two Bills last year, and we have one before us now, and the same words are in them.
That is also a power company, it is an undertaking, and it defines the undertaking. The charter defines the undertaking.

It is an undertaking that proposes to do the same thing. It is to have a wharf, docks and vessels. If you went before a court with two statutes, one for a power company and the other for a millers' association, surely the court would decide that there must be some difference of meaning between a business and an undertaking; and if they both mean the same thing, would it not be better to have one phraseology applying to all? Then there would be no doubt, it would be understood both by the people and by the court.

Section 3, paragraph (a) says:
Carry on the business of purchasing, selling, storing, shipping, &c.
If you were to say, ' carry on the undertaking of purchasing, selling, storing, shipping, &c.' the word ' undertaking ' would not be apt, it would not be a proper word to use in that connection. Therefore we are, in the first place, authorizing this company to carry on the business of selling, -that is ordinarily spoken of as a business; we do not speak of a railway undertaking as a business in the same sense as merchandizing. Then when you come to paragraph (b) you provide that for the purpose of enabling the company the better to carry on its business, which by the previous clause it is authorized to carry on, it may charter vessels, &c. Therefore the word ' business ' is much more apt, it seems to me, than the word ' undertaking ' in a Bill of this character.

I would ask the Finance Minister in reference to subsection (a) of section 3, the latter part:
May construct, acquire, operate, hire, lease, sell or otherwise dispose of elevators for elevating wheat, grain or other products, and acquire, lease, and utilize hydraulic, electric or other power for the purpose of the said business, and generally may carry on an elevator or storage business.

I desire to ask the Finance Minister, who is aware that the grain growers had a delegation here lately waiting upon the government in regard to the government taking over terminal elevators, and operating them under government control, would this Bill, under that clause, confer certain rights on this company, that might prove embarrassing to the government in carrying out that policy, and entail expense? Are you giving rights under this Bill that would have to be purchased by the government should the government decide to accede to the request of the grain growers?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My impression is that we would not. This is simply an enabling Bill which authorizes them to do certain things which an individual might do for himself, and which they are permitted to do in their corporate capacity. I do not think the Bill would create any vested rights that we would have to purchase. Possibly the company might think they would have such rights.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I would like to have an explanation of the provisions of this section 3.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps the Bill had better stand.

I did not understand that the Becancour wharf item had passed.
That was carried.

Well, my hon. friend invited me to criticise each one of these items, a task which I did not feel disposed to undertake, but we asked a couple of questions in regard to this wharf at Becancour. My hon. friend knows that we found out that this wharf was being built tC accommodate Mr. ROCHE.
the Delaware & Hudson railway. I asked who had petitioned for this wharf, and the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Lemieux) told me that it had been asked for by the Delaware & Hudson Railway Company. My hon. friend1 the Minister of Public Works knows the country well'enough to know that at Three Rivers we have three of our own railways, the Canadian Pacific railway, the Canadian Northern railway and the Transcontinental railway, built by ourselves, the others having been largely subsidized by the country. It is in order to permit the Delaware & Hudson Railway Company to get the wood of the Three Rivers district across the St. Lawrence, put it on its cars and take it to the United States, probably pulp wood, that this wharf is being built. In reality we are building the wharf to accommodate an American railway which is depriving these three railways at Three Rivers of their wood freight. I just submit to my hon. friend whether this is a carefully considered and wise policy. My hon. friend the Postmaster General-I do not say it to blame him at all- is one of the directors, I believe, in Canada of the Delaware & Hudson Railway Company. I give that as an instance of how far we might go in our criticism if we brought the same examination to bear on each one of these items. I have no desire to delay the minister, in fact, my desire is to abridge what concerns my own province of Quebec, not only for the reason I gave my hon. friend, but my hon. friend knows that there are very few of us from Quebec here to-night; in fact, I feel like one who treads alone a banquet hall deserted, because, apart from the Solicitor General and the hon. member for Dorchester-
If my hon. friend argued very strongly against an item he might persuade me.

I do not like, in the absence of these gentlemen, to criticise items that they have obtained the insertion of in the budget. Since I have been a member of this House I have tried hard, but in spite of every effort I have never succeeded in getting an item into the estimates of the department of my hon. friend, and I am therefore in a very different position from those who can get items in without even having the trouble to be present to explain them. This manner of criticising the estimates is a most unsatisfactory one, and I had hoped that the committee to amend the rules of the House would have given us an opportunity this year of suggesting some change in the way of proceeding with the estimates. I do not believe there is an assembly voting Supply in any part of the world where estimates are put through in this way. There is no such method adopted in any other deliberative and legislative assembly. If I did what I suppose we

used to do in connection with these estimates I would put the same questions as I have put in regard to Becancour with reference to all these other items, covering more than two pages, and I would detain the minister here until very late. Apart from the other objections which I mentioned before the committee rose at six o'clock, I have no desire to do that, and the question suggests itself to me as to whether there would be some easier way of going through these estimates of the province of Quebec, because I cannot assert some things here in the absence of those representing the counties, because what I might say would be open to objection and might very well be corrected if they were here. These two pages of the estimates involve an expenditure of nearly three quarters of a million and, as my hon. friend will admit, lay the foundation for a very much larger expenditure indeed, because many of these undertakings are really beginnings. I do not know if the suggestion 1 am going to make to my hon. friend and the committee is an acceptable one, because we have sitting now for the last time the very important committee on race track betting, we had all agreed to be there, and it was quite unexpectedly that I was called down here. Does the minister think he could lay upon the table a short statement which might be placed in ' Hansard ' giving answers to the questions that are usually put in connection with these estimates, that is, the date and the amount, the original estimate of the work for which he asks a vote, the amount of- the original contract, the name of the contractors, the tenders if called for, when tenders were called for, if called for in the public papers, the expenditure to date, the amount required to finish the work, the revenue received last year, and the amount expended for maintenance last year. All the questions that could be put in this committee, constituted as it is this evening, could not go beyond that. We have- to take up the time and employ the whole paraphernalia of the House to elicit answers to these questions. It seems to me that if the minister could reserve one of these Quebec items, and at some future sitting of the committee lay that statement on the table of the House and place it in ' Hansard ' I would be perfectly satisfied, and I think it would greatly abridge the work of the committee and of my hon. friend. There are two items in these estimates for Quebec to which I would like to . direct my hon. friend's attention. One is an item of $60,000 for improvements on the Richelieu river. That is a considerable item, and it will require some discussion. There is a further item for a deep water wharf at Sorel, for which $86,000 was voted last year, and for which $42,000 is asked this year. As my hon. friend is no doubt aware
that wharf was built and slipped into the river, we are building it over.
In a different way.

Yes. It seems a pity not to go a little into the discussion of these two items. In regard to the others my hon. friend will see that there could be no other questions asked than those I have jotted down in this memorandum. As my hon. friend is not familiar with the province I might be tempted to extend the discussion unduly. The members who represent these counties are not here. I make these suggestions with the desire of abridging the work of the committee and not taking up my hon. friend's time. If this suggestion is practicable, I would not take up the time of the minister and of the committee by asking the self same questions on each item.

I do not think it is proper to accept the suggestion of my hon. friend with regard to the province of Quebec; I think we should have the same rule as to public works in all the provinces. I think it is a good deal of benefit to discuss items; I receive benefit myself from criticisms by both sides of the House. These gentlemen who are familiar with the public work under review' are able to advance arguments in favour of it when criticism is offered. There is the other objection also that the suggestion would mean the postponement of the items for Quebec, because so long as one item stands the resolution cannot be adopted and we are not much further ahead. I am desirous of going on with the Quebec items to-night, because I informed the members from Quebec these items would be under discussion, as I informed other hon. gentlemen that Quebec, Manitoba, and British Columbia items would probably take up the time of the committee. I am sorry my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) has to go to the race track committee.

I have made the suggestion for the convenience of the minister and the committee. This is the last meeting of that committee, we all agreed to be there and I really must attend.
Mr. PUGSLEYL If there is any particular item my hon. friend will wish to discuss he could do so on the vote for the dredging plant in Ontario or Quebec.
My suggestion was with the idea of facilitating the passing of the estimates and not to delay them.

Very well, then we will go on with the Quebec items.
Oabano-landing pier on west side of Lake Temiscouata, $3,500.
This is to cost 83,500, and we expect to finish it with this vote.
Is it by tender?
Probably, but I am not sure.
Why is not the minister sure?
Where the amount is under $5,000 and the resident engineer is of the opinion that the work can be done better and cheaper by day work we sometimes do it that way.
Has there been any report as to whether it is advisable to do it by tender or day work?
No.
Who judges that?
The chief engineer, subject to the decision of the minister.
On what does the chief engineer make up his decision?
It would depend perhaps on the remoteness of the locality and the likelihood of persons wishing to tender.
Is this a remote locality?
Not very.
It is quite a large manufacturing place.

There are a good many who are of opinion that where cribwork is [DOT] to be done, if you get a good foreman who will look after the work and get good timber, you can do it better than by contract. Under the law we have not the same discretion where the work costs over $5,000.
Are you guided by that?
Yes, very largely.
Are there not a great many exceptions?
Not a great many, quite a number. In case of emergency or in cases where it appears that work such as repairing an old wharf can be better done by day work, we do it.
There always have to be exceptional circumstances?
Yes.
That is what the minister says?
Yes, I so interpret the Act.
The minister is guided by that, there must be exceptional circumstances or else the minister conforms to the Act?
That is what the Act says.
I know what the Act says as well as the minister does, but I want to know what you do.
The minister is guided by, and conducts himself under, the Act.
As a matter of fact, unless exceptional circumstances justify departure from the Act, the minister is controlled by the Act?
Yes, the minister would not think of violating the Act.
See him smile.
I have not heard anything so far which would lead me to believe that this work ought not to be done by tender.
I am not aware that I can give any reason why it should not be done by tender in the usual course.
The minister says it is somewhat less expensive to do it by day work with a foreman or inspector; is it the foreman or the inspector the minister relies on?
We usually use the term * foreman,' the words are interchangeable.

Was not a tailor
once employed to superintend some public work?
Which tailor? .
I forget his name, but he was a tailor by occupation, and the scene was in New Brunswick.
That is a long time ago. Under the old. Conservative government, there was a foreman who was an undertaker.
His occupation would seem to fit him better for' the job than if he were a tailor.
The leader of the opposition is referring to the building of the armoury in Sussex, where a tailor was put in command of the work.
My hon. friend (Mr. Daniel) ought not to butt in on this; how long ago was that?
Since this government has been in power.
That is a long time.
Altogether too long. *
I think I have in mind the gentleman the hon. member refers to. He is a thoroughly good, practical man.
A good tailor?
No, a good all round man, who will do what he is called upon to do-faithfully and well.
I may say that this celebrated tailor was kept on inspecting considerably after the work was done, according to the statement of the gentleman who then represented Kings county in the House.
If that was so, it would be very unusual and ought not to take place. I do not think it has taken place in recent years.
You cannot have too much of ia good thing; and if he was as good an inspector as the minister says he was, his services were probably as valuable afterwards as before.
I think my hon. friend from St. John is relying upon his imagination when he makes the statement he does.
My recollection is the same as that of the hon. member for St. John, that the inspector was kept on after the work was done.
I was not relying on my imagination, but on the positive statement of the former member for Kings, which statement will be found in 'Hansard'.
Will the hon. gentleman tell me what that has to do with the wharf at Cabano?
Not the slightest.

It has to do with the general principle we were discussing of carrying on these works by tender oi day work. The minister was relying on inspection, and I observed that it depended on how good the inspection was. I would not consider it consistent with efficient administration that a tailor should be selected for the inspection of an armoury.

The question of the inspection of this work does not come up now. Our effort is always to get practical men, and I think we succeed in getting them. I have not heard complaints in recent years in regard to inspectors.
Cap a l'Aigle-repairs to wharf, $2,400.
This is to provide for repairs to the wharf, as recommended by the resident engineer, Mr. Decary. The total estimated cost is $2,400.
When was the original wharf built?
In 1881 and 1882. It was widened in 1901.
Is it a free port, or are tolls charged?
As it has not been transferred to the Marine Department, no revenue is derived from it.

I know this place well. It is in the county of Charlevoix, and is one of the summer resorts in the St. Lawrence. The government have a steamer plying between River L'Ouelle, St. Irenee, Cap a l'Aigle, Murray Bay and the terminus of one of the branch lines of the Intercolonial railway. It is at the request of the Richelieu Navigation Company that this vote is put in the estimates.
On what principle does the government act in transferring or not transferring wharfs from the Public Works Department to the Marine Department?
There has never been any principle.
Is it not time that there should be one?

It is, but it is a difficult matter to work out. It is now engaging the attention of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and myself. I may say that this is not a new difficulty; it has existed under all governments since confederation. Suppose I transfer this wharf to the Marine Department. It would at once begin to collect tolls. The farmer who takes half a dozen bags of potatoes to the wharf has to pay toll. He goes home and brings a barrel of flour, and on that he has to pay toll. All the tolls in the course of a year do not amount to much, but they are a burden on the farmer. In several cases I have hesitated on this account to make the transfer. We are endeavouring to work out some plan under wnich we would charge a yearly fee to the steamboat owners, so that the farmers would not have to pay any toll. We may work out a solution of the difficulty on some such basis as that.

I think it is desirable that that should be done, because, admitting the existence of what the minister calls a hardship to farmers, it is still rather inequitable that farmers in some parts of the country should be subjected to that hardship, while farmers in other sections are relieved of it. I therefore think some general system should be adopted, and what the minister suggests seems to have some merit in it. It should not be allowed to continue in its present state of confusion.

In my county fishermen who land their fish on the wharf have to pay wharfage dues, which was



not the case until the wharf had been repaired. I do not see why in some sections of the country there should be no wharfage dues charged, while in my county they are charged because, the wharf has been transferred to the Marine Department. One rule should apply to all. I am not particular whether a tariff is charged on this wharf or the one I refer to made free, for the revenue obtained out of the one I refer to is so trifling that it would make little difference if no tolls were charged. The harbour cost the government something over $30,000 and only one boat went there last year.
Did I understand the hon. minister correctly that these wharfs are free while under the Public Works Department, but when transferred to the Department of Marine and Fisheries, dues are charged.
That is right. Does my hon. friend urge that the wharf at Graven-hurst should be transferred to the Department of Marine and Fisheries at once?
It is likely to be long before it is finished unless the work is proceeded with faster.
It will be completed in good time.

The minister's question is hardly a fair one. Last year we had a statute under discussion, and it was understood that a uniform system was going to be adopted which would work almost automatically. Some regular system should apply, and it should not be left to the discretion of the minister, to decide that it will be a hardship to make the transfer in one case and not in another. I understood that last year in many cases the costs of the agent who looked after the collections were quite equal to the amount collected and sometimes far more.
The department pays only 25 per cent of the recipts.

I think there are cases where the wharfingers are not confined to a percentage. I am not in favour at all of any hardships being inflicted which would only result in collecting a very small amount of fees in proportion to the expenditure, but there should be some uniform system adopted.

There was a wharf built by the old government some twenty years ago upon one of the lakes in the eastern townships and it had never been transferred to the Department of Marine and Fisheries and the old government never collected any wharfage. After I had been minister about a year-the wharf had then been built about nineteen years-there was Mr. HENDERSON.
a suggestion made to me to transfer the wharf to the Marine Department. Of course I let it be known that the department would charge tolls. All the people were then up in arms. They said it was a monstrous thing. For nineteen years they had enjoyed under both governments free use of the wharf and now the government was going to impose toll. The result was, whether rightly or wrongly, I did not make the transfer.
That only shows the necessity of some system.

So it does, but it is a difficult thing to work out. There are two wharfs, one in New Brunswick and one in Nova Scotia, that pay one-third of the total tolls collected from wharfs throughout the whole Dominion. One of these wharfs is at Digby and the other at Campbellton.

Last year I drew attention to the condition at Selkirk. The Public Works Department controls the dock at that place. There has been considerable expenditure on that dock, and I understood there was to be some arrangement by which it would come under the control of the Marine and Fisheries Department. I am not anxious to see a change if dues are to be collected, but what does take place is this. There is a wharfinger supposed to be there, but who is a private banker, and he levies, I presume by authority of the department, a certain fee on each steamboat and fishing boat that comes to the dock. I understand he collects something like $300 a year of which the government does not get a cent. It all goes into his pocket and he does no work that I know of. As a rule, the dock is controlled by Captain William Eobert-son, who is the largest lumber shipper in that locality, and you generally find the dock crowded with his lumber. There is no advantage to the government in these tolls which are charged and they are a hardship on the steamboat men. I would just as soon see this fee done away with altogether, and have an absolutely free dock.

I am surprised at my hon. friend's statement, because if a wharfinger has been appointed, that .would imply that the wharf had been handed over to the Marine Department. My department does not appoint any wharfingers.
I may not be correct in saying he is a wharfinger, but he collects the money and keeps it.
Is there a harbour master in Selkirk?

Not that I know of, unless this man acts as harbour master.
